title: Amazon EventBridge
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of amazon eventbridge and its relationship to Messaging and Event-Driven Architectures.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to amazon eventbridge.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn amazon eventbridge in the context of Messaging and Event-Driven Architectures. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Amazon EventBridge matters because it is one part of messaging and event-driven architecture. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Event-driven application path
content_blocks.alt_text: An event is validated, routed to a function or worker, persisted or acknowledged, and observed; retries and dead-letter handling cover failures.
content_blocks.caption: Assume messages can be delivered more than once; design idempotent consumers.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Amazon EventBridge belongs to Messaging and Event-Driven Architectures. Event-driven applications use queues, topics, event buses and streams to decouple producers from consumers. Plan for duplicate delivery, retries, ordering limits and poison messages.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Event buses; Event rules and patterns; Targets; Scheduled and service-generated events. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For amazon eventbridge, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Event buses
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Event rules and patterns
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Targets
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: Scheduled and service-generated events
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Amazon EventBridge”. hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Amazon EventBridge with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Amazon EventBridge is taught as part of Messaging and Event-Driven Architectures.
Event-driven applications use queues, topics, event buses and streams to decouple producers from consumers. Plan for duplicate delivery, retries, ordering limits and poison messages.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
